fields.sample_size: 12 water professionals interviewed individually in 2018 (8 answered on water supply, 6 on wastewater, 8 on stormwater); five interview questions: relevance and ranking of the five most fundamental current policies, ranking of the ten most defining development steps, and two open-ended questions on challenges and suggestions; policy lists curated from a literature review; open answers coded into nine themes
fields.effect_measure: ranking of policies and development steps by 12 respondents and thematic coding of open-ended answers; no inferential statistics
fields.effect_estimate: For water supply, over half of the 22 development steps that interviewees found fundamental for resilience concern securing the water source (quality and quantity); for wastewater the two most important policies are legislation and regulation (the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System and the Clean Water Act of 1972). The most important past steps relate to (i) securing water quantity and quality, (ii) building, operating and managing adequate infrastructure and (iii) relevant legislation and regulation; the most important current policies relate to plans, programmes and system management that advocate resilience. The greatest future challenges are informal rules (people's mindsets and habits), followed by lack of funding and inflexible regulation; resilience is most effectively implemented at the local level. The study concerns resilience of water, wastewater and stormwater services in one city; access, affordability and exclusion outcomes are not measured.
fields.section: Full text (about 25 pages): Abstract; Methods 3-3.1 (interviews, limitations); Results 4.1-4.3 with Figures 6-14; Conclusions and recommendations
fields.exact_location: Methods (interviews and rankings); Results 4.1 (past development steps), 4.2 (current policies), 4.3 (challenges and suggestions); Figure 14 (three levels of policy implementation); Cuadernos de Vivienda y Urbanismo / Colloquia Urbanistica Latina 2(1)

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a qualitative policy case study of resilience policies in Seattle's water services based on a literature review and 12 interviews; read in full text 2026-10-04. Rankings and thematic coding only; the outcome is resilience of service systems, not household access.
